cards.title: Build a three-part email sequence system (welcome, sales/deadline, re-engagement)
cards.summary: Structure the core revenue email flows: a welcome sequence that warms and trains opens, a sales/deadline sequence that converts, and a re-engagement sequence that cleans the list.
cards.use_when: Planning the automated email backbone for a store's list after opt-in — e.g. post-purchase welcome flows, launch sequences for a new product drop, or dormant-subscriber cleanup.
steps: Build the welcome sequence first: 3–8 emails of high value, each containing a CTA or link to more value, that install the belief shifts a customer needs before they will buy from the sales sequence. The source frames this as warming them up to make future money.

Follow with the sales and deadline sequence: open with some value, deliver a belief shift, give a CTA to the product, explain more about the product, then CTA again (the source shows a double CTA in deadline emails).
End the sales sequence with a scarcity/urgency email — a 48-hour deadline worked well for the presenter's clients, which is a case example, not a guaranteed benchmark.

Add a subscriber re-engagement sequence triggered when someone has not opened for roughly 30–60 days: acknowledge they haven't opened, tell them plainly they'll be removed unless they interact, and send it as a 'final email' with an easy opt-back-in.
Length is flexible — three, five, or eight emails all work; what matters is that each sequence does its job.
caveats: Scarcity and re-engagement performance figures cited are the presenter's experience and are not universal benchmarks.
Never run a lifetime discount or perpetual 'expiring' deadline — the source's urgency claims assume a genuinely time-limited offer.

cards.title: Train opens and clicks with value-only welcome emails
cards.summary: Deliver only value in the welcome phase so subscribers learn to open and click, which conditions them to click promotional emails later.
cards.use_when: Writing the first emails after a customer opts in — building the habit formation phase before any promotional send.
steps: Assume you are competing not just with other senders but with TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube; give subscribers a reason to open your email instead of a cat video, so each send needs utility plus some entertainment value.
Put a CTA link in the value emails pointing to more free value — for example a link to a YouTube video — not to a product, so clicks themselves are being trained.
Match tone to your brand: funnier or more serious both work, but include some entertainment value regardless, because the inbox is an entertainment battlefield.

Vary the email function across the welcome sequence: the first email explains why they signed up and what to expect, later ones give value, and one can deliver a belief shift framed as motivation (the source's example tells a persistence story).

Keep promotional links subtle inside value emails if you include them at all — a link dropped inside a normal sentence is a soft sell; spelling out everything they'll learn and why they must buy is a hard sell.
caveats: The 'train them to click' mechanism is the presenter's model, not a measured causal finding.
Soft sells are for value emails; the source still uses hard CTAs in promo sequences — the split is by sequence type, not a rule that all email must be soft.

cards.title: Place a P.S. soft-sell CTA at the end of promo emails
cards.summary: Use a small postscript offer link within an otherwise value-heavy promotional email to keep the ask low-pressure.
cards.use_when: Promotional email or newsletter where you want product exposure without the email reading as a full pitch — e.g. announcing a new product line quietly.
steps: Lead the email body with value or a personal note; keep the promotional mention out of the main copy.
Add a P.S. line announcing the product with one short paragraph and a link: 'we just launched X, here's what it does, click here if you want to know more.'
Treat this as awareness building rather than a conversion push — the goal is making the reader aware the offer exists.
Reserve the explicit, feature-by-feature pitch for the dedicated sales email, where the same source uses hard CTAs.
caveats: The source says nothing is wrong with hard CTAs in promo sends as long as value is also present — the P.S. soft sell is one pattern, not the only acceptable one.

cards.title: Write deadline emails with a duplicated CTA structure
cards.summary: Structure urgency emails by motivating a change, naming the deadline, stacking belief shifts, and repeating the CTA twice.
cards.use_when: Final send of a launch or promotion window where the deadline is real and near.
steps: Motivate the big change first — tell the reader why this decision matters this year, before the ask.
State the deadline explicitly with hours remaining (the source example says 'only 48 hours left').
Follow with more belief shifts that dismantle the objections stopping them from acting.
Repeat the CTA — the source's example tells the reader to join, explains why, then tells them to join again; a double CTA is common in these emails.
Test urgency and scarcity language; the presenter reports it has performed very well across clients, which is a case observation rather than a guaranteed result.
caveats: Only use real deadlines; the source's examples all correspond to genuinely time-limited programs.
Presented performance is anecdotal, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Trigger a re-engagement (reviver) sequence at 30–60 days of inactivity
cards.summary: Automatically send a last-chance email to non-openers to protect deliverability and sender reputation.
cards.use_when: List hygiene: setting up automation on your email service provider to remove or reactivate cold subscribers.
steps: Set the automation trigger at roughly 30 days of no opens (the source gives a 30–60 day window).
Write the email as a plain, honest goodbye: acknowledge the subscriber hasn't been opening, state that this is the last time you'll ask, and offer an easy way to stay.
Include a statement that the list is kept high quality and unengaged contacts will be removed, per the source's examples.
Offer a re-welcome path in a P.S. — 'you're welcome back anytime' — so the removal is not permanent if they choose to engage.
Carefully vet any 'no open in 30 days' window — an unopened email is not proof of disinterest for a store with lower open rates.
caveats: The deliverability rationale (protecting primary-inbox placement, avoiding the promotions tab) is the presenter's model; verify current ESP/ISP behavior for your setup.
The source's own fall into spam came with 1–3% opens, while their healthy list ran 40% opens — both are the presenter's own figures, not norms to target.

cards.title: Set a concrete copywriting goal for each email before writing
cards.summary: Define the action you want the reader to take before writing, then write the email to move the reader toward that one action.
cards.use_when: Every store email — product launch, restock announcement, cart-recovery follow-up, or content email.
steps: Write the single intended action in one sentence (open the link, reply, click the offer, register).

Choose the sequence email type most suited to that action: utility/welcome email for new subscribers, value email for engagement training, soft sell for awareness, hard CTA for direct sales, deadline email for urgency.
Do not over-pack the email with multiple competing CTAs — the source specifically notes one example where the sender didn't ask much, just gave value and one subtle CTA.
Use one idea per email; the presenter's sequence model has one email function per send.
If a beginner can't write a sequence of eight, start with three and add more later — the source says this is fine.
caveats: Sequence length is flexible; the source does not claim an optimal number of emails.

cards.title: Use a subject line at or under 40 characters
cards.summary: Keep subject lines short enough not to truncate on mobile.
cards.use_when: Writing subjects for any store email — restock, launch, deadline, re-engagement.
steps: Aim for roughly 40 characters or fewer; the source notes longer subjects get cut off in mobile previews, leaving only the first few words plus ellipsis.
Cut filler words that don't change meaning — the source's bad example ran 60–70 characters.
Avoid generic subjects that telegraph the email body — the source criticizes 'Transform your business with a hands-free marketing funnel' because the reader already knows what they'll read.
Check the first visible words on a phone-sized preview, since that is all many recipients will see.
caveats: 40 characters is the presenter's stated heuristic; treat it as a starting point, not a universal rule.
No specific open-rate improvement from shorter subjects is claimed in the source.

cards.title: Structure an automated branch by engagement level
cards.summary: Use if/else automation so more engaged subscribers receive promotional paths and less engaged ones receive more value.
cards.use_when: Designing email automations for a store's post-signup or post-purchase flow on an ESP.
steps: Choose a trigger: subscribing to a list, submitting a form, opening an email, clicking an email, visiting a web page, or a tag being added.
Send the first email, then add a wait step or an if/else condition — the source says wait and if/else are the two you'll use most.
Branch on engagement, e.g. 'if they have opened any email in the last 30 days' — the source's example branch sends one email to openers and another ('why no click') to non-openers.

Guide openers down a shorter path to the promo; give non-openers more value first — the presenter's model is that the more engaged someone is, the more receptive they are to promotion, so promote less to the unengaged.
Start simple: if this is your first automation, send a second welcome email to non-openers and a promo to openers instead of building a complex tree.
caveats: This engagement-based promotion principle is the presenter's model, not a measured result.
Interface naming (trigger names, wait step) is ActiveCampaign-specific — the source demonstrates it there; another ESP will differ, so verify current menus.

cards.title: Choose an email service provider by requirement, not brand loyalty
cards.summary: Pick the ESP that fits your feature needs and budget rather than defaulting to the most expensive one.
cards.use_when: Selecting or migrating the email platform for a store, or auditing a client's existing stack.
steps: The presenter's ranking: ActiveCampaign is most capable by far and most expensive (over $2k/month in the source's own case), ConvertKit is cheaper with fewer features, Mailchimp is mid-priced with a clunky interface in the source's opinion, and Kajabi/ClickFunnels include email as a basic add-on with limited automation depth.
Weigh automation complexity against cost — the source treats intricate automations as the main reason to pay for a top-tier ESP.
If a client already has an ESP, use theirs; the source says the specific tool matters less than the sequence strategy.
Learn the tool via the vendor's own tutorials — the source notes software companies provide ample documentation because they need users to keep the product.
Verify each platform's current pricing and features, as these change.
caveats: Pricing and feature comparisons reflect the presenter's experience at time of recording; they are not stable inputs.

cards.title: Copy the structure of top performers' video sales letters
cards.summary: Write a VSL by researching high-performing examples in the niche, stealing the structure, and filling it with your own offer's specifics.
cards.use_when: Writing a video sales letter or long-form sales page for a store's hero product.
steps: Find the top businesses in your niche and study how they structure their VSLs — the source says the same structure recurs across examples and structure itself can be taken.
Fill the proven structure with your own audience call-out, problem, outcome, mechanism pillars, proof, credibility, and offer.
Keep the copy 'plug and play' — the source's repeated point is that VSLs are templates.
Do the writing work yourself; the source dismisses asking 'how do I write one' when examples are available to model.
caveats: Do not copy the actual claims, testimonials, or stats of another business — only the structural sequence.

cards.title: Name the unique mechanism so the product is not a commodity
cards.summary: Create a named special feature that makes the product meaningfully different and defendable against comparison shopping.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a product page, VSL, or ad where the product is easily price-compared against near-identical alternatives.
steps: Identify one distinct feature or system and give it a name (the source points to named systems like 'Money Magnet System').
Frame it as the thing that avoids the common failure of competitors — the source's vacuum example is a V12 engine that doesn't lose suction as the bin fills, versus weaker one-cylinder machines.
Draw the commodity-vs-mechanism contrast: a plain winter tire gets bought on price, a 'rubber stud technology' tire supports a higher price because it is not the same thing.
Use the mechanism to answer the implicit objection — the source's resistance-training example explicitly addresses 'why wouldn't I just use free weights?'
Keep the claim grounded in a real product feature; the source invents examples only for illustration, and a fabricated mechanism is a legal and trust risk.
caveats: The purpose is differentiation, not deception — invent a name for a real feature, don't invent the feature.
This is a copywriting frame and does not by itself make a product superior.

cards.title: Use a standard VSL structure: call-out through offer
cards.summary: Sequence a video sales letter through audience call-out, problem, failed alternatives, mechanism, proof, credibility, and CTA.
cards.use_when: Scripting a flagship VSL or long-form sales page for a hero product or high-ticket service.
steps: Call out the specific avatar and their urgent problem; the source's example opens with 'attention online fitness coaches' and a big promise with a dollar figure.
Show what most people do and why it doesn't work — throw stones at alternatives with proof and analogies to make the comparison easy to understand.
Deliver the belief shift: what actually works, why it's better, and how to use it.
Present the unique mechanism's two to three main pillars and explain why your way is effective while alternatives are inferior, using analogies throughout.
Stack proof: results, testimonials, borrowed authority, stats, then your own credibility and cost narration (what you spent to learn the method).
End with a CTA and, where appropriate, the unique selling proposition — tell them what to do and why now; the source notes a VSL is essentially a collection of emails in one asset.
caveats: The example VSL shown is for a coaching business; adapt the audience, problem, and proof to your product category rather than copying its claims.
Testimonials show what others achieved — they are not a promised result.

cards.title: Sell the thing that sells the thing
cards.summary: Don't just pitch the product — sell the mechanism or method that makes the product the obvious choice.
cards.use_when: Writing any sales asset where the product looks like every other option in the category.
steps: Define the system or mechanism the product delivers and make it the centerpiece of the copy, not the product name alone.
Walk through why the mechanism works — the source shows the VSL spending most of its runtime explaining the named system before asking for the purchase.
Contrast it with the common alternative (organic outreach, paid ads, inferior machines) and name the specific reason those fail.
Once the reader believes the mechanism works, the offer becomes a lower-friction decision — the source describes this as the point where working with them becomes a no-brainer.
In ecommerce terms: sell the reason your formulation, sourcing, or design works before selling the SKU, so price comparison loses its grip.
caveats: The source's example is a high-ticket coaching funnel; the same principle is transferred here to ecommerce, not demonstrated there.

cards.title: Do avatar and problem research before writing the VSL
cards.summary: Anchor the sales letter in a specific avatar's fears, obstacles, wants, and day-in-the-life before drafting copy.
cards.use_when: Starting a new VSL, landing page, or ad for a category you don't know intimately.
steps: Define exactly who the offer is for, and research their fears, obstacles, wants, and desires; write out what their day might look like.
Identify the urgent problem your product solves in their life — not a general benefit.
Define the dream outcome the product helps them achieve.
Lay out the step-by-step process to that outcome, then build two or three pillars of the unique mechanism explaining why this way works and alternatives are inferior.
Use analogies throughout the mechanism section so the explanation is simple to understand.
caveats: No specific research methods are given in the source; use your own customer data (reviews, support tickets, surveys) to fill this out.

cards.title: Be a stat shower, not a claim-maker
cards.summary: Replace bare claims with concrete evidence, because readers translate unsupported claims into disbelief.
cards.use_when: Any ad, PDP, or email line that asserts quality, speed, results, or superiority.
steps: Identify every unsupported claim in the draft ('it works', 'best formula') and flag it.
Replace each with proof — a number, a result, a demonstration, or a testimonial — that the reader can see and check.
Use borrowed authority (quotes, credible sources) and stats that support the point you're making.
Frame testimonials as evidence of what others achieved rather than claims you are making yourself.
Keep the proof specific to your own genuine results; the source's figures (125 coaches, five over $1M) belong to that business and shouldn't be borrowed.
caveats: Do not fabricate statistics or results — only use verifiable proof from your own business or legitimately cited third parties.

cards.title: Use AI to improve and generate ideas, not to write the copy
cards.summary: Use AI for line-level improvement, analogy generation, and ideation while the actual structure and judgment stay with you.
cards.use_when: Speeding up copy drafting for emails, PDPs, ads, or VSLs without producing obvious AI output.
steps: Write the copy yourself first, then prompt 'make this better / funnier / more clever' and take only the lines that are actually better than yours.

Use prompt patterns like 'what are some questions you can ask me that can get me the best result', 'give me one-line analogies that explain how X is as [adjective] as Y', 'give me quotes that explain X', and 'give me stats that prove why X'.
Iterate with refinement prompts — 'make them shorter', 'add some funny ones too', 'make them more simple, one-liners' — before using anything.
Keep prompts simple rather than hunting for elaborate prompt chains.

Never copy long-form AI output about your product or customers — the source warns against it on quality and credibility grounds; treat AI as a tool that requires your skill to operate, like a calculator needs a mathematician.
caveats: The presenter states AI will not replace copywriting skill and describes what was, at the time, ChatGPT's weak copy output; model capabilities and best prompts change, so re-test.
Fabricated or recycled analogies and stats must be checked for accuracy and fit before publication.

cards.title: Avoid the telltale AI analogs and clichés in copy
cards.summary: Detect and remove the recycled phrases that make copy read as machine-generated and lazy.
cards.use_when: Editing any AI-assisted or self-written ad, email, or PDP copy before publishing.
steps: Scan for overused analogy families — the source flags magic wands and baking a cake as the ones AI reaches for most.
Cut robotic openers like 'I hope this message finds you well' — the source points out no friend texts you that way.
Remove generic hype that shifts no belief and gives no value ('imagine having a steady stream of clients').
Rewrite so the copy sounds like a person speaking to a friend, which is what the source says copy is for.
Read the copy aloud and flag anything you would not actually say to a customer in person.
caveats: If AI-assisted phrasing survives editing because it fits your voice, the source's concern is about unedited paste-in, not AI use itself.

cards.title: Build a landing page with blocks, background, and readable text
cards.summary: Assemble a one-goal landing page from drag-and-drop blocks with a subtle background treatment.
cards.use_when: Building a signup page or sales page for a store campaign without hiring a designer.
steps: Choose the page's one goal — signup (opt-in page) or purchase (sales page); remove all extra navigation like About or Contact.
Build with drag-and-drop blocks: place the hero section at top, then two-column text, then closing text and form. Add a video block and a form block as needed.

Add a background image rather than leaving the page plain white or black — the source searched '4K black and red background' and used that, and favored pages with a subtle gradient or visual treatment.
Layer a dark color over the background with reduced opacity so the headline text stays readable while the image stays visible; increase opacity toward solid for maximum contrast.
Edit directly in the blocks — text, fonts, sizes — the source compares it to editing a Word document and insists no coding is involved.
caveats: The source notes plain white backgrounds have made millions of dollars for some businesses — the background treatment is the presenter's preference, not a proven rule.
The interface shown is ActiveCampaign's builder; other tools differ, so verify current UI.

cards.title: Match landing page tool to budget and feature needs
cards.summary: Select a landing page builder by visual quality, feature depth, and cost rather than defaulting to one platform.
cards.use_when: Choosing or recommending the page-builder stack for a store's campaign or launch.
steps: Use Miro to map the funnel visually before building pages — the source describes it as a funnel mapping tool.
Consider Carrd for a limited free option, or Google Docs to sketch a page's visual layout when nothing else is available.
Use Kajabi or ClickFunnels when you need the most common, feature-rich options — the source calls them somewhat expensive at roughly a couple hundred dollars a month, far less than a top-tier ESP.
Don't let cost deter you: the source argues page builders are drag-and-drop and anyone who can use Zoom or Discord can build a page.
Skip AI landing-page generators — the source finds editing generated pages slower than starting from scratch.
caveats: Pricing and feature summaries are the presenter's at time of recording and should be re-verified.
Free versions like Carrd's have very limited features.

cards.title: Map the sequence to lead temperature (cold to hot)
cards.summary: Sequence email types from welcome to value to soft sell to hard sell while the subscriber warms up.
cards.use_when: Planning the timeline of a new-subscriber or post-purchase email series.
steps: Sketch a simple timeline: day one welcome email, day three value, day five soft sell, day eight hard sell — the source's illustrative model.
Track lead temperature conceptually: cold subscribers don't know you and won't buy, hot subscribers know you well and might buy.
Pair with automation branching: openers can skip ahead to the soft sell, non-openers get more value first.
Increase promotion only as engagement rises — the source's principle is more engaged subscribers are more susceptible to promo, and less engaged ones should be promoted to less.
Apply the same cold-to-hot logic to any automation, not just welcome sequences.
caveats: The day markers are an illustration, not a tested cadence; treat them as a starting skeleton.
The engagement-promotion relationship is a stated principle, not a measured finding.
